analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal funding for the EPA's science and research account.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to a House committee and to a subcommittee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Matt Salmon proposed a one-sentence bill saying no federal money could ever be appropriated for the Environmental Protection Agency's Science and Technology account. That account pays for the EPA's own research, testing, monitoring, and the scientific analysis behind air and water standards. The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by the EPA — such as fossil fuel and chemical operations — would benefit from a drastically weakened EPA, since the agency would lose the in-house science it uses to identify pollution problems, set exposure limits, and defend standards against challenge. Taxpayers would see a modest budget saving, though at the cost of the science that underpins enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any appropriation of funds for the EPA's Science and Technology account, eliminating the agency's core research, monitoring, and assessment funding.

The EPA uses the Science and Technology account to fund the laboratory work and risk assessments behind air, water, and chemical standards; removing it would make it far harder for the agency to identify pollution problems or defend its rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through reduced monitoring of air and water quality, weaker scientific grounding for pollution limits, and slower EPA response to contamination — effects that fall hardest on communities near industrial sites. EPA scientists and laboratories would lose funding wholesale.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and EPA science staff

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the bill would argue that the EPA's science budget is large, that some research is duplicative of work done by other agencies or outside scientists, and that taxpayers should not fund an office they view as supporting overregulation.

The honest cost for anyone who supports cutting EPA spending: eliminating the entire account, rather than trimming it, would remove the independent research the agency needs to set defensible pollution limits, likely inviting legal challenges and leaving gaps in monitoring that states cannot easily fill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a small budget saving in exchange for dismantling the EPA's entire in-house science operation. Because EPA research is the basis for air and water protections that most Americans rely on, the cost to the public of this approach is far larger than the savings, and the bill attracted no cosponsors in the House.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Science Committee and then to its Environment subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without ever being debated or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Salmon introduced the bill on June 18, 2015, with a single provision: no funds may be appropriated for the EPA's Science and Technology account.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology on the day it was introduced.
Two months later, on August 18, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, and no further action appears in the record.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill was never voted on, so it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the public kept the EPA's science and monitoring programs intact, and regulated industries gained nothing they would have gotten from a weakened EPA. The only tangible change was that a one-member bill with no cosponsors failed to advance, which is the normal course for legislation with that little support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone who relies on EPA science

for.name: Rep. Matt Salmon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill proposing to eliminate all appropriations for the EPA Science and Technology account.

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at committee and its Environment subcommittee without a markup or vote; the bill's only actions were the two referrals.

against.name: House colleagues of Rep. Salmon
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill; it ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the sole sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors from either party, so there is no roll-call record of a partisan split.

industries.industry: Polluting industries (fossil fuels, chemicals, heavy manufacturing)
industries.note: A fully defunded EPA science operation would mean less monitoring, testing, and risk analysis of industrial pollution, easing the scientific basis for enforcement and standards. The industry's gain would come directly at the public's expense.

industries.industry: EPA science and research enterprise (federal laboratories and environmental researchers)
industries.note: The bill would eliminate the entire Science and Technology account, which funds the EPA's laboratories, monitoring, and research staff. The work those scientists do is the same work that protects public health.
